question: How should the advance placement of warning signs be determined?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Advance placement of warning signs is a Guidance (recommended) matter based on providing adequate Perception-Response Time. For permanent warning signs, Table 2C-3 gives recommended advance placement distances keyed to the posted or 85th-percentile speed and the condition being warned of (Condition A: speed reduction/lane changing in heavy traffic; Condition B: deceleration to a listed advisory speed). For temporary traffic control (TTC) zones, signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at distances that vary with roadway type, condition, and posted speed (e.g., 4–8 times the speed limit on urban streets, 8–12 times on rural highways, and ½ mile or more on freeways and expressways). Guidance (recommended): - Warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed; where a series of two or more advance warning signs is used, the closest sign should be placed approximately 100 feet for low-speed urban streets to 1,000 feet or more for freeways and expressways (see Table 6B-1). - On freeways and expressways, advance warning sign placement should be longer because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow, extending as far as ½ mile or more. - On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone, in feet, should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end of the range used when speeds are relatively high; when two or more advance warning signs are used on higher-speed streets, the advance warning area should extend a greater distance. - On rural highways, the effective placement of the first warning sign should be substantially longer—8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph—and the advance warning area should extend 1,500 feet or more for open highway conditions. - The effectiveness of the placement of warning signs should be periodically evaluated under both day and night conditions; Table 2C-3 provides guideline distances by posted or 85th-percentile speed for Condition A (speed reduction and lane changing in heavy traffic) and Condition B (deceleration to a listed advisory speed). - Per Table 2C-3's notes, for warning signs with less than 6-inch legend or more than four words, a minimum of 100 feet should be added to the advance placement distance to provide adequate legibility. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] shows Table 2C-3, "Guidelines for Advance Placement of Warning Signs," listing recommended distances (e.g., 225 ft at 20 mph up to 1,600 ft at 85 mph for Condition A) with footnotes explaining legibility-distance adjustments and PRT/deceleration assumptions. - [Image 2] shows Section 2C.04, Placement of Warning Signs, with the Guidance that signs should provide adequate PRT and that Table 2C-3 distances should be applied with engineering judgment, along with the full Table 2C-3. - [Image 3] shows Sections 6H.01–6H.02, including the Guidance that TTC advance warning signs should be placed at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed, per Table 6B-1. - [Image 4] shows Figure 2C-2 (horizontal alignment curve example), whose notes direct users to Table 2C-3 for advance placement distance guidelines. - [Image 5] shows Section 6B.04, Advance Warning Area, with the Guidance on 4–8 times the speed limit for urban streets, 8–12 times for rural highways, and ½ mile or more for freeways and expressways. Citations: - Section 6H.02 Guidance §1 (p.798) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §3 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §4 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §6 (p.771) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §5 (p.152) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §804 (p.153) - Table 2C-3 (p.152)
gold_answer: Warning signs should be placed to provide adequate perception-response time. Table 2C-3 is an aid, but its distances should be applied with engineering judgment and can be adjusted for roadway features, other signing, and visibility.
